sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 17

answer.explanation: A /26 leaves six host bits, so the block has 64 addresses. In the specified block, .64 is the network and .127 the broadcast; usable hosts span .65–.126 inclusive, totaling 62. The question asks usable hosts, not block size, and /31 point-to-point exceptions do not apply.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Thirty-two is not the usable count of this /26 block; /26 has 64 total addresses.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Sixty-four is the total block size before network/broadcast reservations.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Six host bits give 64 total addresses minus two reservations, leaving 62 usable hosts.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Thirty usable hosts is the /27 result, not /26.

evidence.quote: For ordinary broadcast LANs let h=32-p. Total addresses=2^h; usable hosts=2^h-2, reserving network and directed broadcast. Find the changing octet’s increment as 256-mask octet, round the address down to a multiple, and extend through the next boundary minus one.

192.168.2.64/26 spans .64–.127; usable .65–.126 gives 62 hosts. 192.168.10.25/28 spans .16–.31, so its network is .16. 172.17.128.0/21 spans 172.17.128.0–172.17.135.255; .128.255 and .135.0 are valid interior hosts, but .135.255 is broadcast. /27 gives 32 total and 30 usable, not 32 usable.

questions.stem: Which OSI layer is responsible for establishing, maintaining, and ending communication sessions?
questions.hint: Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 18

answer.explanation: The stem explicitly specifies communication sessions, matching the OSI session role rather than merely a TCP connection. NET19 assigns dialog management and checkpoints to that layer. Transport serves process endpoints, application supplies services and presentation handles representations. B is therefore the specific reference-model lifecycle role.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Transport connection state is distinct from the explicitly named OSI session/dialog lifecycle.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Session manages dialogs and their setup, maintenance and recovery/end lifecycle.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Application supplies user/application network services rather than the distinct session-layer lifecycle.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Presentation translates/compresses/encrypts representations instead of managing dialogs.

evidence.quote: OSI session roles establish/manage dialogs and can coordinate checkpoints so transfer resumes after interruption. Presentation roles translate encodings and handle compression/encryption. Compression reduces representation size; encryption hides content and need not shrink it. Application protocols provide services directly to applications. Practical implementations distribute these functions differently; TLS is not proof of a separate physical presentation-layer device.

TCP establishes state with SYN, SYN+ACK, then ACK. SYN consumes one sequence position even with no application bytes. An acknowledgment states the next expected sequence number. For client ISN=395 and server ISN=260: client sends SYN seq395; server sends SYN+ACK seq260 ack396; client sends ACK seq396 ack261. Later byte counts advance sequence numbers. FIN also consumes one sequence position.

questions.stem: A bus topology network has 20 nodes. If the main cable breaks, what happens?

options.label: A
options.text: Only the two nodes nearest the break are affected

options.label: B
options.text: The network continues to function normally

options.label: D
options.text: Only the node that caused the break is disconnected

questions.hint: Draw the links and identify shared components, alternate paths and the effect of the specified failure or growth requirement.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 19

answer.text: A main-backbone break can disrupt the whole basic bus segment
answer.explanation: In the conventional single-backbone bus assumed by these options, a main-cable break disrupts the shared segment, affecting the network rather than just one endpoint. NET08 qualifies the physical mechanism as an unterminated break. Redundant segmentation or protected designs are not specified, so C expresses the standard basic-bus failure consequence.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A main-backbone fault affects shared signaling, not merely the two closest nodes.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: A broken unterminated backbone does not preserve normal basic-bus operation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The shared basic bus segment can fail as a whole when its main backbone is broken.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A backbone break differs from an isolated endpoint spur failure and need not be limited to one node.

evidence.quote: Bus uses a shared backbone; an unterminated break can disrupt the segment. Star connects endpoints through a central device: one edge failure isolates that endpoint, whereas central failure affects the star. Ring forms a loop; basic single rings are vulnerable to a break, while protected dual rings differ. Token passing is associated with Token Ring but is an access method, not a necessary property of every ring. Tree is hierarchical; hybrid combines arrangements.

questions.stem: Synchronous data transmission differs from asynchronous in that synchronous transmission:

options.label: A
options.text: Uses start and stop bits for each data chunk

options.label: B
options.text: Sends data continuously with sender and receiver using the same clock

questions.hint: Use the cited note definitions to identify the requested function or scope, then check each alternative against that same rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 20

answer.text: Ongoing synchronized clock recovery rather than per-character start/stop
answer.explanation: NET06 contrasts character start/stop framing with ongoing clock recovery in synchronous transmission. B is the intended synchronized-transfer description; “same clock” should mean synchronized timing, not necessarily a single physical clock device. The note gives no universal speed ordering, and both methods can transmit digital/binary data.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Per-character start/stop bits describe character-oriented asynchronous serial transmission.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Synchronous transfer maintains coordinated timing through ongoing clock recovery rather than character start/stop framing.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: No universal slower-than-asynchronous rule follows from the timing method.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Synchronous framing can carry binary data; the timing convention does not prohibit it.

evidence.quote: Simplex is one way, half duplex alternates directions, and full duplex permits simultaneous sending/receiving. A walkie-talkie is half duplex; a telephone conversation uses full duplex. Serial sends sequential bits; parallel uses multiple conductors and may suffer skew. Character-oriented asynchronous serial adds start/stop bits; synchronous framing uses ongoing clock recovery. Neither is synonymous with browser asynchronous requests.

questions.stem: What is the PRIMARY function of the Network Layer (Layer 3)?

options.label: C
options.text: End-to-end routing of data between different networks using IP addresses

questions.hint: Match the requested scope or data unit to the layer duties in the note; distinguish hop delivery from end-to-end process delivery.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 21

answer.text: Logical IP addressing and routing across networks
answer.explanation: NET12 gives network-layer logical addressing and routing; NET11 explains forwarding IP packets among networks by destination prefixes. C directly states that responsibility. The other options assign physical signaling, link MAC/error detection and session-dialog management, which belong to different model layers.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Transporting raw physical bits/symbols is the physical-layer function.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: MAC addressing and hop frame error detection are data-link responsibilities.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Network-layer logical addressing and routing carry IP packets between networks.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Establishing application dialogs is a session-layer role rather than IP routing.

evidence.quote: Routers forward IP packets between networks using destination prefixes and next hops. They separate broadcast domains and normally do not forward local link broadcasts. A default gateway is usually a router, while a protocol gateway can translate application formats; therefore a gateway is not inherently a device that implements every OSI layer.

Sending proceeds from application data to transport segment/datagram, network packet, link frame and physical bits/symbols; receiving reverses the order. Each layer serves the layer above. A router removes a received link frame, inspects IP, and creates a new link frame for the next hop. MAC addresses usually change across routed hops; end-to-end IP addresses ordinarily remain until translation.

OSI session roles establish/manage dialogs and can coordinate checkpoints so transfer resumes after interruption. Presentation roles translate encodings and handle compression/encryption. Compression reduces representation size; encryption hides content and need not shrink it. Application protocols provide services directly to applications. Practical implementations distribute these functions differently; TLS is not proof of a separate physical presentation-layer device.

questions.stem: Which of the following IPv4 addresses is INVALID?
questions.hint: Separate address width, syntax, reserved scope and the supplied prefix or historical classful convention.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 22

answer.explanation: An IPv4 decimal octet must fit eight bits, from 0 through 255. D has 256 and is therefore syntactically invalid. A–C each meet that range condition. B’s .255 ending alone does not establish a broadcast without a prefix, so it cannot be rejected merely by its last octet.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: All four octets are within 0–255, so this notation is valid.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Every octet is valid; a .255 ending alone does not determine broadcast status without a prefix.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: All four values fit eight-bit octets and form valid dotted-decimal notation.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The second octet 256 exceeds the maximum representable eight-bit value 255.

evidence.quote: Write IPv4 as four decimal octets 0–255, or as 32 binary bits. Use weights 128,64,32,16,8,4,2,1 within each octet. Thus 11000001 10000011 00011011 11111111 is 193.131.27.255. A value such as 257 is impossible. Syntactic validity differs from assignability: an address ending .0 or .255 can be a host under some prefixes.

questions.stem: In IPv6, addresses are how many bits long?
questions.hint: Separate address width, syntax, reserved scope and the supplied prefix or historical classful convention.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 23

answer.explanation: NET23 explicitly gives IPv6 addresses a 128-bit width. IPv4 uses 32 bits; 64 may describe a common subnet interface boundary but is not the whole IPv6 address length. Ninety-six bits is likewise not the full width. D therefore answers the requested address size.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Thirty-two bits is the IPv4 address width, not IPv6.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Sixty-four bits is not the complete IPv6 address width.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ninety-six bits does not match the specified 128-bit IPv6 address length.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: IPv6 addresses contain 128 bits as explicitly stated in NET23.

evidence.quote: IPv6 has 128-bit hexadecimal addresses, flexible prefixes and no IPv4-style broadcast. Sources, not routers, fragment IPv6 packets. IPv6 does not automatically encrypt traffic or make authentication unnecessary. Compare IPv6’s larger 128-bit address space and encryption support separately; specify the property being evaluated.

IP supplies connectionless best-effort packet delivery, not end-to-end ordering or retransmission. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits. Its minimum header is 20 bytes and can grow to 60 bytes; it is not a 32-bit header. IHL counts 32-bit words; total length includes header and payload. TTL limits lifetime across routers; the protocol field identifies TCP, UDP or another upper-layer protocol.

A common IPv6 unicast subnet uses a 64-bit subnet prefix and a 64-bit interface identifier. This split does not make the complete address 64 bits: it remains 128 bits. Special uses and explicitly different prefix lengths must be considered separately.

questions.stem: A bridge decides whether to forward a frame to another network segment by examining the:

options.label: A
options.text: IP address in the packet header

options.label: B
options.text: Port number in the segment header

questions.hint: Compare signal repetition, frame forwarding, packet routing and policy enforcement using the stated device or traffic assumptions.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 24

answer.text: Learn source MACs and forward according to destination MAC
answer.explanation: A bridge learns which sources are reachable through each port and consults the destination MAC when forwarding/filtering a frame. C names the relevant link addresses. IP, transport ports and TTL belong to higher-layer packet/segment processing, not the ordinary bridge forwarding decision. Unknown destinations may be flooded, so learning does not imply always-one-port forwarding.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Destination IP prefixes drive routing, not ordinary layer-2 bridge frame forwarding.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Transport ports identify process endpoints and are not the bridge MAC-table lookup key.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Source MAC informs learning and destination MAC informs forwarding/filtering to the appropriate segment.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: TTL is an IP header field used in routed packet lifetime, not ordinary bridging.

evidence.quote: A bridge or ordinary Ethernet switch operates at layer 2. It learns source-MAC-to-port mappings, looks up the destination, forwards a known unicast to its port, filters it if the destination is on the incoming segment, and floods an unknown unicast or broadcast within its VLAN. A switch does not always send only to one destination port. Wireless access points normally bridge wireless and wired link-layer traffic.

Ports identify transport endpoints; the application can choose a transport and request socket buffer sizes, subject to OS limits. A TCP connection is identified by source/destination IP and source/destination port, with TCP understood. IPv4 protocol numbers identify upper protocols; 80 is a usual HTTP port, not an IP protocol number. Clients often use ephemeral ports. SCTP is a reliable message-oriented transport with multiple streams.

IP supplies connectionless best-effort packet delivery, not end-to-end ordering or retransmission. IPv4 addresses are 32 bits. Its minimum header is 20 bytes and can grow to 60 bytes; it is not a 32-bit header. IHL counts 32-bit words; total length includes header and payload. TTL limits lifetime across routers; the protocol field identifies TCP, UDP or another upper-layer protocol.

questions.stem: Circuit switching guarantees bandwidth for the duration of a call. What is the main DISADVANTAGE of this?

options.label: B
options.text: Bandwidth is wasted when no data is actively being transmitted

options.label: C
options.text: Packets may arrive out of order

questions.hint: Compare signal repetition, frame forwarding, packet routing and policy enforcement using the stated device or traffic assumptions.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 25

answer.text: Reserved bandwidth can be wasted during silence
answer.explanation: Circuit switching holds resources for the call even while endpoints are silent, so unused reservation cannot be statistically shared as packet traffic would be. B gives that cost. Circuit switching does not inherently deliver packets out of order or prevent voice transmission; traditional telephone calls are a standard example.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Reserved circuits can offer predictable transfer behavior; setup cost is distinct from universally high transfer latency.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Capacity remains reserved during silence and can be wasted when no data is sent.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Independent out-of-order packet routing is not the defining reserved-circuit disadvantage.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Traditional telephone calls are the note’s standard circuit-switching example, so voice is supported.

evidence.quote: Circuit switching sets up a path with reserved resources, transfers data, then releases it. Predictable allocated bandwidth trades against setup/blocking and wasted reservation during silence. A traditional telephone call is the standard example. Packet switching divides data into packets that share links statistically; queueing can add variable delay and loss. This does not make modern voice-over-packet impossible: buffering, scheduling and capacity planning manage it.

questions.stem: Under the textbook direct line-of-sight wireless-link convention, which option gives the most complete set of listed technologies whose direct path can be blocked by buildings or terrain? Treat radio waves as the broad category rather than assuming every radio propagation mode needs line of sight.
questions.hint: Compare the signal mechanism, medium properties or transmission direction against the definitions and stated physical assumptions.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 26

answer.text: Microwave and infrared under the conventional line-of-sight assumption
answer.explanation: Conventional directional microwave links need suitable path visibility, and infrared generally does not penetrate walls. Obstacles can therefore interrupt the direct links specified here. Both individual technologies fit, so the combined option is the complete response. Radio waves is a broader physical category that includes microwave but also other propagation modes; the question does not assert that all radio links share the same line-of-sight restriction.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The broad radio category includes propagation modes beyond the specified line-of-sight comparison.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Microwave fits the stated direct-link case, but this alone omits infrared.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Infrared fits the stated obstructed-direct-path case, but this alone omits microwave.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Both microwave and infrared fit the specified comparison, making this the complete set.

evidence.quote: Radio, microwave and infrared are unguided media. Ground waves follow Earth, sky waves can reflect from ionized layers, and line-of-sight paths require suitable visibility. Microwaves are radio waves in the broader physical classification. Infrared generally does not penetrate walls. Directionality depends on antennas: omnidirectional means broad azimuth coverage, not equal radiation in every 3-D direction. Legacy Ethernet straight-through cables join unlike MDI/MDI-X roles; crossover joins like roles, such as PC–PC or switch–switch. Auto-MDI-X can remove that requirement.

questions.stem: What does CIDR stand for, and what problem did it solve?

options.label: A
options.text: Classless Inter-Domain Routing; it solved address wastage in classful addressing

options.label: B
options.text: Classful Internet Domain Routing; it solved packet loss

options.label: C
options.text: Centralized IP Domain Routing; it solved routing loops

options.label: D
options.text: Classless Internet Data Routing; it solved latency in WANs

questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 27

answer.text: Classless Inter-Domain Routing; flexible prefixes reduce rigid class allocation waste
answer.explanation: CIDR replaces rigid class allocation. Flexible prefixes allow blocks sized to requirements and aggregation of aligned blocks, addressing waste from fixed historical class sizes. The other expansions are incorrect and their proposed packet-loss, loop or latency cures are not the defined purpose.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: This gives the correct expansion and relates flexible prefix allocation to avoiding rigid class-size waste.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Classful Internet Domain Routing is the wrong expansion, and CIDR is not defined as a packet-loss cure.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Centralized IP Domain Routing is not the acronym expansion or the stated mechanism.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Classless Internet Data Routing is incorrect; CIDR is not defined as a general WAN-latency cure.

evidence.quote: CIDR, Classless Inter-Domain Routing, replaces rigid class allocation and supports aggregation. Combine contiguous aligned blocks sharing leading bits; unrelated adjacent-looking labels may not aggregate cleanly. Four consecutive /26 blocks covering a /24 summarize to /24. More-specific routes must remain available where the aggregate would otherwise send traffic to the wrong next hop.

For H hosts, choose the smallest h satisfying 2^h-2≥H, then p=32-h. For 24 hosts use /27; 52 or 57 use /26; 100 use /25; 500 use /23. For at least six equal subnets choose b=3. A Class C /24 split to /27 yields eight subnets. Always check both the number of subnets and the host capacity.

questions.stem: How many subnets are created when you borrow 5 bits from the host portion of a Class B network?
questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 28

answer.explanation: Borrowing five bits yields 2^5=32 equal subnets under modern counting. The parent Class B /16 would become /21, but the direct subnet count only needs the specified five borrowed bits. NET26 says not to subtract two subnets under modern practice.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Five is the number of borrowed bits, not the exponential number of resulting subnet combinations.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Sixteen subnets would use four borrowed bits rather than five.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Five borrowed bits have 32 distinct combinations and therefore produce 32 subnets.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sixty-four subnets would require six borrowed bits.

evidence.quote: To split parent /a into equal /p blocks, borrow b=p-a bits and obtain 2^b subnets. Do not subtract two subnets under modern practice. For a Class B /16 parent split to /19, b=3 gives eight subnets, each with 8192 addresses and 8190 conventional hosts. A /19 alone does not state its parent.

questions.stem: The 'forwarding table' in a bridge is also known as the:
questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 29

answer.explanation: The bridge forwarding database records MAC-to-port associations learned from source addresses and used for destination lookups. MAC table is therefore the matching name. A routing table maps IP prefixes to next hops; ARP associates on-link IPv4 addresses with link addresses. Those are different tables even if one device maintains several of them.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Routing tables describe destination IP prefixes and next hops rather than bridge MAC-to-port mappings.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: ARP caches associate IPv4 next hops with link addresses, not MAC addresses with bridge ports.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The bridge’s learned source-MAC-to-port forwarding database is its MAC table.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: IP table does not name the layer-2 learned MAC forwarding database described in NET10.

evidence.quote: A bridge or switch’s MAC address table is its learned forwarding database: it associates MAC addresses with ports for frame forwarding. It differs from an ARP cache, which associates an IPv4 next hop with a link address, and from a routing table, which selects next hops for IP prefixes.

A bridge or ordinary Ethernet switch operates at layer 2. It learns source-MAC-to-port mappings, looks up the destination, forwards a known unicast to its port, filters it if the destination is on the incoming segment, and floods an unknown unicast or broadcast within its VLAN. A switch does not always send only to one destination port. Wireless access points normally bridge wireless and wired link-layer traffic.

questions.stem: Which layer of the OSI model is responsible for defining voltage levels, cable specifications, and how bits are physically transmitted?
questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 30

answer.explanation: Voltage, cable/interface characteristics and signal transport are the physical-layer scope in NET09. Data-link functions operate on frames and MAC access, network handles IP routing and transport handles process delivery. The wording explicitly asks how bits are physically represented and carried, so C is the corresponding layer.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Data link manages frames/access rather than defining the physical voltage and cable interface.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Network manages logical addressing/routing rather than electrical signal specifications.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Physical-layer specifications include connectors, signaling, voltage and timing.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Transport supplies process delivery rather than cable and voltage definitions.

evidence.quote: A NIC supplies a computer’s network interface and commonly implements both physical and link functions. Calling a NIC a physical interface does not mean all its functions are layer 1. Physical specifications include connectors, signaling, voltage, timing and physical coding/modulation; the PHY interface to MAC handles hardware signaling.

Sending proceeds from application data to transport segment/datagram, network packet, link frame and physical bits/symbols; receiving reverses the order. Each layer serves the layer above. A router removes a received link frame, inspects IP, and creates a new link frame for the next hop. MAC addresses usually change across routed hops; end-to-end IP addresses ordinarily remain until translation.

questions.stem: In a star topology, what happens if the central hub fails?

options.label: A
options.text: Only the hub's nearest neighbor is affected

options.label: C
options.text: The network continues operating in bus mode

options.label: D
options.text: Nodes automatically reconnect in ring topology

questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 31

answer.text: The dependent star loses connectivity when its center fails
answer.explanation: In a basic star every endpoint depends on the central hub for communication with other endpoints. Failure of that common center therefore affects the whole star. No alternate center or automatic topology reconfiguration is specified; the network does not become a bus or ring merely because the hub stops functioning.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The center serves all star endpoints, so its failure is not limited to the nearest neighbor.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: All endpoints depend on the central hub, so the basic star loses inter-endpoint connectivity.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A hub failure does not physically or logically rewire the star into an operational bus.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: No automatic ring reconnection mechanism follows from the basic star topology.

evidence.quote: Bus uses a shared backbone; an unterminated break can disrupt the segment. Star connects endpoints through a central device: one edge failure isolates that endpoint, whereas central failure affects the star. Ring forms a loop; basic single rings are vulnerable to a break, while protected dual rings differ. Token passing is associated with Token Ring but is an access method, not a necessary property of every ring. Tree is hierarchical; hybrid combines arrangements.

questions.stem: What type of noise CANNOT be completely eliminated because it is caused by the random motion of electrons due to temperature?
questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 32

answer.explanation: The stated cause—random motion associated with temperature—is thermal noise in NET06. Crosstalk is neighboring-channel coupling and impulse noise is a short disturbance. D names a different noise phenomenon not defined by random thermal motion. The cause identifies C without requiring a claim that all other real noise can be perfectly eliminated.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Crosstalk arises from coupling between nearby communication channels, not the stated thermal-motion cause.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Impulse noise is a short disturbance rather than persistent random thermal motion.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Thermal noise is explicitly caused by random thermal motion, matching the temperature-dependent clue.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: This option does not match the random thermal-motion definition supplied in NET06.

evidence.quote: Attenuation reduces signal strength. Distortion changes shape, often because frequencies have different delays. Noise adds unwanted energy: thermal noise comes from random thermal motion, crosstalk leaks from nearby channels, and impulse noise is a short disturbance. Amplifiers amplify noise too; digital repeaters regenerate decisions but cannot reconstruct every corrupted bit.

Intermodulation distortion occurs when multiple signals interact through a nonlinear component and generate unwanted combination-frequency products. Its mechanism differs from random thermal motion, adjacent-channel leakage and an isolated impulse disturbance.

questions.stem: Which IP address class has a first-octet range of 128–191?
questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 33

answer.explanation: NET22 gives first-octet 128–191 for historical Class B, corresponding to leading bits 10. Ordinary Class A is 1–126, Class C is 192–223 and Class D uses leading 1110 for multicast. Since the question explicitly asks classes, the historical categorization is appropriate rather than inferring a current CIDR prefix.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Ordinary historical Class A uses first octets 1–126 rather than 128–191.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Historical Class B spans first octets 128–191, with leading bits 10.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Historical Class C spans 192–223, above the supplied interval.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Class D multicast begins with 1110, outside the Class B 128–191 interval.

evidence.quote: Historical classes use leading patterns: A 0 with /8, B 10 with /16, C 110 with /24; D 1110 is multicast and E 1111 reserved. Ordinary class-A first octets are 1–126 because 0 and 127 have special uses. B spans 128–191 and C 192–223. Default usable counts are 2^24-2, 2^16-2 and 254. Modern CIDR requires the actual prefix and overrides class defaults.

questions.stem: The Session Layer's 'checkpointing' feature means that it:

options.label: A
options.text: Encrypts data to protect it from interception

options.label: B
options.text: Compresses data to reduce transmission time

options.label: C
options.text: Saves the state of a communication session at regular intervals so it can be resumed after interruption

options.label: D
options.text: Translates data between different character encoding formats

questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 34

answer.text: Checkpoint state supports resuming after interruption
answer.explanation: A checkpoint records recoverable progress/state so interrupted work can resume from an agreed point. NET19 assigns such coordination to the session role. Encryption, compression and encoding translation belong to representation handling and do not by themselves preserve resumable dialog progress. C matches the checkpoint recovery purpose.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Encryption conceals content and does not define saving resumable session progress.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Compression reduces representation size rather than recording recovery checkpoints.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Saving agreed progress/state enables continuation after interruption rather than restarting from the beginning.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Encoding translation changes representation format, not checkpoint recovery state.

evidence.quote: OSI session roles establish/manage dialogs and can coordinate checkpoints so transfer resumes after interruption. Presentation roles translate encodings and handle compression/encryption. Compression reduces representation size; encryption hides content and need not shrink it. Application protocols provide services directly to applications. Practical implementations distribute these functions differently; TLS is not proof of a separate physical presentation-layer device.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a De Jure standard?

options.label: A
options.text: A manufacturer's proprietary cable format adopted industry-wide

options.label: B
options.text: A standard officially approved by ISO or IEEE

options.label: C
options.text: A standard developed by a single corporation without regulatory approval

options.label: D
options.text: A protocol widely used but never formally documented

questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 35

answer.explanation: NET03 defines de jure by formal approval. B directly states official approval, while industry adoption without that approval is de facto. Corporate origin does not alone decide status, but C specifically lacks formal approval and D emphasizes informal use. Therefore B is the option establishing the defining approval condition.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Widespread adoption alone demonstrates de facto use rather than formal de jure approval.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Official approval matches the defining de jure criterion in NET03.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A corporate format without the stated formal approval does not meet the offered de jure definition.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Widespread informal use without formal approval is de facto rather than de jure.

evidence.quote: Protocol syntax defines message structure, semantics defines field meanings, and timing defines when/how fast exchanges occur. A standard supports interoperability. De facto means established through use; de jure means formally approved. ISO develops international standards; IEEE develops LAN standards such as 802.3 and 802.11; ITU-T develops telecommunications standards. ANSI coordinates US standards, EIA is associated with interface standards, and FCC is a regulator.

questions.stem: Parallel data transmission sends multiple bits simultaneously. Its key DISADVANTAGE compared to serial transmission is:

options.label: B
options.text: It cannot be used for digital data

options.label: C
options.text: It requires more transmission lines and can suffer from interference between lines

options.label: D
options.text: It only works over fiber-optic cable

questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 36

answer.explanation: Parallel transfer needs several conductors to carry simultaneous bits. Those paths can experience skew and neighboring-channel coupling, as NET06’s impairment definitions explain. C states the extra-line and interference burden. No universal slower-speed claim, inability to carry digital data or fiber-only restriction follows from parallel transmission.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Parallel is not universally slower; performance depends on implementation, distance and synchronization.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Parallel transmission can carry digital bits simultaneously, exactly as the stem states.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Multiple conductors add wiring and can suffer skew or coupled interference between adjacent lines.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Parallel transmission is not restricted to fiber and commonly concerns multiple electrical conductors.

evidence.quote: Simplex is one way, half duplex alternates directions, and full duplex permits simultaneous sending/receiving. A walkie-talkie is half duplex; a telephone conversation uses full duplex. Serial sends sequential bits; parallel uses multiple conductors and may suffer skew. Character-oriented asynchronous serial adds start/stop bits; synchronous framing uses ongoing clock recovery. Neither is synonymous with browser asynchronous requests.

Attenuation reduces signal strength. Distortion changes shape, often because frequencies have different delays. Noise adds unwanted energy: thermal noise comes from random thermal motion, crosstalk leaks from nearby channels, and impulse noise is a short disturbance. Amplifiers amplify noise too; digital repeaters regenerate decisions but cannot reconstruct every corrupted bit.

questions.stem: A packet-switching network may be UNSUITABLE for real-time voice communication because:

options.label: B
options.text: Variable latency and possible packet loss can disrupt real-time audio

options.label: D
options.text: All bandwidth is reserved, leaving none for voice

questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 37

answer.text: Variable delay and packet loss can disturb real-time audio
answer.explanation: Real-time audio is sensitive to late or missing data. Packet networks may introduce variable queueing delay and loss, so B gives a plausible suitability issue. Modern voice over packets remains possible with buffering, scheduling and capacity planning; it is not intrinsically prohibited or dependent on reserved circuits.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Datagram packet switching does not require a dedicated circuit before every communication.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Variable queueing latency and loss can make audio arrive late or incomplete.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: NET31 explicitly allows voice over packets with suitable engineering.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Statistical link sharing differs from reserving all bandwidth for established circuits.

evidence.quote: Circuit switching sets up a path with reserved resources, transfers data, then releases it. Predictable allocated bandwidth trades against setup/blocking and wasted reservation during silence. A traditional telephone call is the standard example. Packet switching divides data into packets that share links statistically; queueing can add variable delay and loss. This does not make modern voice-over-packet impossible: buffering, scheduling and capacity planning manage it.

TCP offers a reliable ordered byte stream using sequence numbers, acknowledgments, retransmission and windows. Flow control protects the receiver; congestion control protects network capacity. UDP sends independent datagrams with ports and a checksum but no built-in setup, delivery guarantee, retransmission or ordering. Live interactive traffic may choose UDP when late data is less useful than lost data. Application protocols can add reliability over UDP.

questions.stem: For a Class C network subnetted to /27, how many usable hosts per subnet are available?
questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 38

answer.explanation: A /27 leaves five host bits regardless of the historical class of its parent. Those bits provide 32 total addresses. On an ordinary broadcast subnet, network and broadcast reserve two, leaving 30 usable host addresses. Parent classification matters for subnet counting, not this explicit-prefix host calculation.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Thirty-two is the total address count before reserving network and broadcast.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Five host bits give 32−2=30 ordinary usable hosts.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Twenty-eight does not follow from the stated five host bits and two standard reservations.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Sixty-two usable hosts corresponds to /26 rather than the supplied /27.

evidence.quote: For ordinary broadcast LANs let h=32-p. Total addresses=2^h; usable hosts=2^h-2, reserving network and directed broadcast. Find the changing octet’s increment as 256-mask octet, round the address down to a multiple, and extend through the next boundary minus one.

questions.stem: Which routing type sends data to the NEAREST of multiple hosts sharing the same IP address?
questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 39

answer.explanation: Anycast routes to one member of a set sharing the address, typically the nearest by routing metrics. That is not necessarily geographic distance. Multicast targets a subscribed group, broadcast all in scope and ordinary unicast a single designated destination. D uniquely matches the shared-address nearest-member rule.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Multicast targets a subscribed group rather than selecting only one nearest shared-address member.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Broadcast targets all destinations within its scope, not the nearest member.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Ordinary unicast targets one designated destination without the shared-address nearest-member semantics.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Anycast selects one shared-address member, normally nearest according to routing metrics.

evidence.quote: Flooding sends copies on eligible outgoing links with duplicate/lifetime controls; random walk picks a neighbor probabilistically. Unicast targets one destination, broadcast all in a scope, multicast a subscribed group and anycast one member sharing an address, normally nearest under routing metrics. Multi-destination packets can list multiple targets; this is not necessarily identical to broadcast. Group multicast trees use mechanisms such as reverse-path checks; Ethernet spanning tree is a different layer-2 mechanism.

questions.stem: The term 'coaxial' refers to the fact that the cable's inner conductor and outer shield:

options.label: A
options.text: Are made of the same conductive material

options.label: D
options.text: Are both covered in plastic insulation

questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 40

answer.text: The conductor and shield share an axis
answer.explanation: The name coaxial refers to a common geometric axis for the inner conductor and surrounding shield. NET07 states this directly. Neither identical material, opposite signal directions nor a particular insulation covering defines the term; those are separate construction or usage details rather than the shared-axis relationship.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The definition concerns geometric arrangement, not whether both conductive parts use the same material.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: The inner conductor and outer shield share a central axis, giving the coaxial name.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Opposite signal directions are not the defining common-axis geometry.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Insulation details do not define coaxial; sharing an axis does.

evidence.quote: Twisted pairs reduce coupled interference; UTP has no added shield and STP adds shielding. Coax has an inner conductor and outer shield sharing an axis. Fiber guides light and resists electromagnetic interference; it supports high capacity and long reach, but requires suitable optics and installation. Exact speed, cost and reach depend on the specification, not the material alone. Fiber can still be tapped.

questions.stem: Which option best describes a protocol-translating gateway joining unlike networked systems?

options.label: A
options.text: A device that boosts signal strength over long distances

options.label: B
options.text: A device that connects networks using the same protocol

options.label: C
options.text: A device that connects two or more networks using different protocols, topologies, or architectures

options.label: D
options.text: A device that filters traffic based on MAC addresses

questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 41

answer.text: A device that connects two or more networks using different protocols, topologies, or architectures
answer.explanation: Gateway has several networking meanings. A default IP gateway is commonly a router, while a protocol gateway translates between unlike protocols or application formats. The question asks for that translating role, so the option joining unlike systems fits. Signal regeneration belongs to repeaters, same-protocol routing does not require translation, and MAC-based filtering describes bridging or switching rather than protocol conversion.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Signal regeneration/strength extension is a repeater function rather than either gateway meaning defined here.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Connecting networks using the same protocol describes routing without the required protocol translation.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: A protocol gateway joins unlike systems through the translation required by the stated scope.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: MAC-address frame filtering describes bridging/switching rather than the gateway distinction in NET11.

evidence.quote: Routers forward IP packets between networks using destination prefixes and next hops. They separate broadcast domains and normally do not forward local link broadcasts. A default gateway is usually a router, while a protocol gateway can translate application formats; therefore a gateway is not inherently a device that implements every OSI layer.

A bridge or ordinary Ethernet switch operates at layer 2. It learns source-MAC-to-port mappings, looks up the destination, forwards a known unicast to its port, filters it if the destination is on the incoming segment, and floods an unknown unicast or broadcast within its VLAN. A switch does not always send only to one destination port. Wireless access points normally bridge wireless and wired link-layer traffic.

A repeater regenerates layer-1 signals without inspecting destination addresses. An active hub is a multiport repeater: it repeats incoming signals onto other ports, placing half-duplex endpoints in one collision domain. A passive hub is a connector. A hub neither learns MAC addresses nor eliminates collisions. An endpoint such as a network printer consumes services; routers, hubs and access points are intermediary devices.

questions.stem: An organization is assigned the Class A IP address 10.200.240.4. What is the network address?
questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 42

answer.text: 10.0.0.0 under the explicitly requested Class A default
answer.explanation: Because the question explicitly assigns Class A, its historical default /8 supplies the intended network/host boundary. Keep first octet 10 and zero the remaining 24 host bits to obtain 10.0.0.0. If a different CIDR prefix were supplied it would override the default, but none is given in this class-specific question.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: The Class A /8 default keeps first octet 10 and clears the remaining three octets.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: This assumes a /16 boundary instead of the explicitly invoked Class A /8 default.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: This assumes /24, retaining host bits that the Class A default would clear.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Clearing the network octet too loses the assigned Class A network identifier 10.

evidence.quote: Historical classes use leading patterns: A 0 with /8, B 10 with /16, C 110 with /24; D 1110 is multicast and E 1111 reserved. Ordinary class-A first octets are 1–126 because 0 and 127 have special uses. B spans 128–191 and C 192–223. Default usable counts are 2^24-2, 2^16-2 and 254. Modern CIDR requires the actual prefix and overrides class defaults.

Compute network=address AND mask. Host bits zero identify the block start; host bits one give broadcast. With 172.16.28.252/20, the third octet is grouped in blocks of 16, so the network is 172.16.16.0 and broadcast 172.16.31.255. A written host/prefix such as 172.105.180.0/21 need not be an aligned block label: masking yields 172.105.176.0/21.

questions.stem: UTP cable is most susceptible to which type of interference?
questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 43

answer.explanation: UTP is unshielded copper: twisting reduces coupled interference but does not remove all electromagnetic coupling. NET06 identifies crosstalk as leakage from nearby channels. B names the relevant ordinary interference types, whereas thermal-only excludes other sources and infrared/gamma are not the note’s cabling-susceptibility mechanism.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Thermal noise is not the only impairment; unshielded pairs can experience coupled electromagnetic interference.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: EMI and adjacent-pair/channel crosstalk are relevant to unshielded copper, though twisting reduces coupling.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Infrared is an optical/unguided signaling category rather than the stated ordinary copper-coupling issue.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Gamma radiation is not the interference mechanism identified for UTP in the supplied note.

evidence.quote: Twisted pairs reduce coupled interference; UTP has no added shield and STP adds shielding. Coax has an inner conductor and outer shield sharing an axis. Fiber guides light and resists electromagnetic interference; it supports high capacity and long reach, but requires suitable optics and installation. Exact speed, cost and reach depend on the specification, not the material alone. Fiber can still be tapped.

Attenuation reduces signal strength. Distortion changes shape, often because frequencies have different delays. Noise adds unwanted energy: thermal noise comes from random thermal motion, crosstalk leaks from nearby channels, and impulse noise is a short disturbance. Amplifiers amplify noise too; digital repeaters regenerate decisions but cannot reconstruct every corrupted bit.

questions.stem: For a known unicast whose destination is on a different learned switch port in the same VLAN, what is the main forwarding difference between an active hub and an ordinary Ethernet switch?

options.label: A
options.text: Hubs operate at Layer 3; switches operate at Layer 2

options.label: B
options.text: Hubs send data to all connected devices; switches send data only to the intended device

options.label: C
options.text: Hubs use IP addresses; switches use MAC addresses

options.label: D
options.text: Hubs support fiber-optic; switches do not

questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 44

answer.text: Hubs send data to all connected devices; switches send data only to the intended device
answer.explanation: An active hub repeats incoming signals onto its other ports without examining addresses. A switch learns MAC-to-port mappings and, for the specified known unicast on another port, forwards the frame only to that destination port. Unknown unicasts and broadcasts are different cases and can be flooded. The scope restriction makes the intended contrast accurate without treating selective forwarding as a universal rule for all switch traffic.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Hubs are layer-1 repeaters, not layer-3 routers; ordinary switches are layer 2.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: In this known-unicast case the hub repeats to other ports, while the switch sends only to the learned destination port.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Hubs do not use IP addresses to decide forwarding; they repeat signals without address inspection.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Hub versus switch is a signal-repetition versus frame-forwarding distinction; it does not impose the claimed prohibition on optical switch links.

evidence.quote: A bridge or ordinary Ethernet switch operates at layer 2. It learns source-MAC-to-port mappings, looks up the destination, forwards a known unicast to its port, filters it if the destination is on the incoming segment, and floods an unknown unicast or broadcast within its VLAN. A switch does not always send only to one destination port. Wireless access points normally bridge wireless and wired link-layer traffic.

A repeater regenerates layer-1 signals without inspecting destination addresses. An active hub is a multiport repeater: it repeats incoming signals onto other ports, placing half-duplex endpoints in one collision domain. A passive hub is a connector. A hub neither learns MAC addresses nor eliminates collisions. An endpoint such as a network printer consumes services; routers, hubs and access points are intermediary devices.

Ethernet switches can have fiber-optic interfaces with suitable optical transceivers. A forwarding role therefore does not impose a copper-only restriction: distinguish what the device does with frames from the physical medium used by its ports.

questions.stem: In multicast routing, data is sent to:

options.label: A
options.text: All devices on the network regardless of interest

options.label: C
options.text: The nearest host among multiple hosts sharing an address

options.label: D
options.text: Only the devices that have expressed interest in receiving the data

questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 45

answer.explanation: NET30 distinguishes multicast group delivery from unicast, broadcast and anycast. Receivers express membership/interest in a group, rather than every network device receiving by definition or only one nearest destination being selected. D matches that destination-set meaning. Delivery still depends on the deployed network’s forwarding and membership mechanisms.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: All devices regardless of interest describes broadcast scope rather than multicast group selection.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: One specific destination is ordinary unicast rather than a receiver group.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: One nearest shared-address member is anycast.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Multicast targets a subscribed group of receivers that expressed interest.

evidence.quote: Flooding sends copies on eligible outgoing links with duplicate/lifetime controls; random walk picks a neighbor probabilistically. Unicast targets one destination, broadcast all in a scope, multicast a subscribed group and anycast one member sharing an address, normally nearest under routing metrics. Multi-destination packets can list multiple targets; this is not necessarily identical to broadcast. Group multicast trees use mechanisms such as reverse-path checks; Ethernet spanning tree is a different layer-2 mechanism.

questions.stem: What IPv4 address class is designed for multicast addressing?
questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 46

answer.explanation: Historical IPv4 Class D begins with bits 1110 and is designated for multicast. Classes A, B and C describe historical unicast network allocations, with differing default prefixes. The question explicitly asks that historical class designation, so D is supported independently of how modern unicast prefixes are allocated.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: Class A is historical unicast network space rather than the multicast class.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Class B is historical unicast space with a /16 default, not multicast.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Class C is historical unicast space with a /24 default.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Class D, identified by leading 1110, is designated for IPv4 multicast.

evidence.quote: Historical classes use leading patterns: A 0 with /8, B 10 with /16, C 110 with /24; D 1110 is multicast and E 1111 reserved. Ordinary class-A first octets are 1–126 because 0 and 127 have special uses. B spans 128–191 and C 192–223. Default usable counts are 2^24-2, 2^16-2 and 254. Modern CIDR requires the actual prefix and overrides class defaults.

questions.stem: Which OSI layer provides sequencing, acknowledgments and receiver flow control for end-to-end reliable process delivery, as in TCP?
questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 47

answer.explanation: TCP uses sequence numbers, acknowledgments and windows to provide reliable ordered delivery between transport endpoints. Reliable link protocols can use similar mechanisms, but their scope is a single hop. The explicit end-to-end process requirement therefore selects transport. IP supplies best-effort network delivery, while session coordinates dialogs and checkpoints rather than defining TCP’s ordered-byte-stream reliability and receiver flow control.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: IP is best effort and does not supply the listed reliable acknowledgment/retransmission service.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Data-link reliability is hop-local rather than the required end-to-end process service.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: Transport supplies TCP’s end-to-end sequencing, acknowledgments and receiver flow control.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: Session manages dialogs/checkpoints rather than the specifically listed link/TCP reliability machinery.

evidence.quote: TCP offers a reliable ordered byte stream using sequence numbers, acknowledgments, retransmission and windows. Flow control protects the receiver; congestion control protects network capacity. UDP sends independent datagrams with ports and a checksum but no built-in setup, delivery guarantee, retransmission or ordering. Live interactive traffic may choose UDP when late data is less useful than lost data. Application protocols can add reliability over UDP.

Controlled access uses polling, reservations or a token to grant turns; correctly coordinated access avoids contention collisions. Channelization divides frequency, time or code resources. Stop-and-wait sends one frame and waits for ACK, retransmitting on timeout; sequence bits distinguish duplicates. Sliding windows permit multiple unacknowledged frames. Link reliability/flow control is hop-local; transport reliability/flow control is end-to-end. Ethernet detects corruption but does not itself guarantee reliable delivery.

OSI session roles establish/manage dialogs and can coordinate checkpoints so transfer resumes after interruption. Presentation roles translate encodings and handle compression/encryption. Compression reduces representation size; encryption hides content and need not shrink it. Application protocols provide services directly to applications. Practical implementations distribute these functions differently; TLS is not proof of a separate physical presentation-layer device.

questions.stem: For the IP address 192.168.2.64/26, what is the broadcast address?
questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 48

answer.explanation: A /26 has blocks of 64 addresses. Starting at .64, this block runs through .127; the final address has all six host bits one and is broadcast. .65 and .126 are ordinary first/last hosts. .255 belongs to another /26 block, so it is not this subnet’s broadcast.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: 192.168.2.65 is the first usable host, not the all-host-bits-one address.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: 192.168.2.126 is the last usable host, one address below broadcast.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: The .64–.127 /26 block ends at .127, its directed broadcast.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: The .255 address is outside this .64–.127 subnet block.

evidence.quote: 192.168.2.64/26 spans .64–.127; usable .65–.126 gives 62 hosts. 192.168.10.25/28 spans .16–.31, so its network is .16. 172.17.128.0/21 spans 172.17.128.0–172.17.135.255; .128.255 and .135.0 are valid interior hosts, but .135.255 is broadcast. /27 gives 32 total and 30 usable, not 32 usable.

Compute network=address AND mask. Host bits zero identify the block start; host bits one give broadcast. With 172.16.28.252/20, the third octet is grouped in blocks of 16, so the network is 172.16.16.0 and broadcast 172.16.31.255. A written host/prefix such as 172.105.180.0/21 need not be an aligned block label: masking yields 172.105.176.0/21.

questions.stem: Which of the following CORRECTLY describes the role of SMTP?

options.label: A
options.text: Translates domain names to IP addresses

options.label: B
options.text: Governs how web pages are requested and delivered

options.label: C
options.text: Governs how email messages are sent from a client to a mail server

options.label: D
options.text: Enables file transfer between devices over the internet

questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 49

answer.explanation: NET21 assigns SMTP mail submission and relay. A client sending a message to a mail server is therefore a correct SMTP role. DNS resolves names, HTTP serves web requests and FTP transfers files. This does not assign end-user mailbox retrieval to SMTP; POP3/IMAP serve that separate task.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: DNS resolves domain names to address records rather than SMTP.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: HTTP governs web requests/responses, not SMTP.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: SMTP submits mail from a client to a server and relays messages between mail servers.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: File transfer is the FTP service role in this comparison, not SMTP’s defining mail role.

evidence.quote: HTTP defines web request/response semantics; it is stateless, and a message body may be absent. HTTPS adds TLS protection. FTP transfers files using control and separate data connections; it is not the same protocol as SFTP. SMTP submits and relays mail; POP3 retrieves messages and IMAP accesses/synchronizes server mailboxes. Saying SMTP handles both sending and end-user mailbox retrieval is inaccurate.

DNS resolves names to records, including IPv4 A and IPv6 AAAA addresses; it can use UDP or TCP port 53. DHCP dynamically leases IPv4 settings, commonly address, mask, gateway and DNS server. Its basic exchange is discover, offer, request, acknowledge. IP itself does not assign addresses.

questions.stem: An omnidirectional antenna transmits signals in which pattern?

options.label: A
options.text: A narrow beam toward a specific target

options.label: C
options.text: In all directions simultaneously, creating 360-degree coverage

options.label: D
options.text: In a focused line-of-sight path only

questions.hint: Apply the cited definitions to the stated scope; for calculations, derive the result from the supplied prefix, bit count or resource rule.
sources: Data Communication & Networking review questions · Question 50

answer.text: 360-degree azimuth coverage, with a nonuniform vertical pattern
answer.explanation: NET07 defines omnidirectional as broad azimuth coverage. C is correct when its 360 degrees refers to the horizontal plane, not equal power in every three-dimensional direction. Directional beams or upward-only radiation do not describe this pattern. Antenna elevation patterns can still have lobes/nulls, so the answer retains that scope qualification.

choices.label: A
choices.explanation: A narrow targeted beam is directional rather than omnidirectional azimuth coverage.

choices.label: B
choices.explanation: Upward-only radiation does not provide the broad around-the-antenna azimuth pattern.

choices.label: C
choices.explanation: 360-degree azimuth coverage is the intended meaning, without asserting equal power in all three-dimensional directions.

choices.label: D
choices.explanation: A single focused path describes a directional antenna pattern.

evidence.quote: Radio, microwave and infrared are unguided media. Ground waves follow Earth, sky waves can reflect from ionized layers, and line-of-sight paths require suitable visibility. Microwaves are radio waves in the broader physical classification. Infrared generally does not penetrate walls. Directionality depends on antennas: omnidirectional means broad azimuth coverage, not equal radiation in every 3-D direction. Legacy Ethernet straight-through cables join unlike MDI/MDI-X roles; crossover joins like roles, such as PC–PC or switch–switch. Auto-MDI-X can remove that requirement.

notes.title: Bit rate, baud and channel capacity

blocks.text: Bit rate R is bits/second; a bit interval is 1/R. Baud is symbols/second, not necessarily the number of voltage transitions.
With M equally encoded symbol states, each symbol can carry log2(M) bits; R=baud×log2(M), before coding overhead.
Binary Manchester uses extra transitions, so binary does not universally mean baud equals bit rate.
For an ideal noiseless channel, Nyquist gives R≤2B log2(M).
For Gaussian noise, Shannon gives C=B log2(1+S/N), with a linear power ratio; SNR(dB)=10 log10(S/N).
Bandwidth, signal levels and noise appear explicitly.
Distance affects attenuation, delay and often achievable rate, but is not a separate variable in these simplified capacity formulas.
Worked example

items.text: B=3000 Hz and M=4 give a 12,000 bit/s noiseless limit. If S/N=15, Shannon also gives 3000×log2(16)=12,000 bit/s. Do not insert 15 dB as a linear ratio.

For this legacy MAC interface, the relevant sublayer is PLS.
This name is architecture-specific: other PHY designs use reconciliation (RS), physical coding (PCS), physical medium attachment (PMA) and related sublayers.
Do not present PLS as a universal OSI sublayer name.
IEEE 802.3 10GBASE-ER architectures, David Law
A bridge or ordinary Ethernet switch operates at layer 2.

It learns source-MAC-to-port mappings, looks up the destination, forwards a known unicast to its port, filters it if the destination is on the incoming segment, and floods an unknown unicast or broadcast within its VLAN.
A switch does not always send only to one destination port.
Wireless access points normally bridge wireless and wired link-layer traffic.
Each switch port separates collision domains; full-duplex point-to-point Ethernet has no collisions and does not use CSMA/CD.
Switching permits independent conversations simultaneously.
Broadcasts still reach the VLAN unless another control filters them.
A layer-3 switch also routes, so device marketing names do not override the function being examined.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module
Routers forward IP packets between networks using destination prefixes and next hops.
They separate broadcast domains and normally do not forward local link broadcasts.
A default gateway is usually a router, while a protocol gateway can translate application formats; therefore a gateway is not inherently a device that implements every OSI layer.
A firewall allows, rejects or inspects traffic under a security policy; it does not necessarily encrypt.
A VPN, Virtual Private Network, provides a logical private connection over another network; a secure VPN authenticates/encrypts its tunnel.
A modem modulates outgoing and demodulates incoming carrier signals.
These functions may coexist in one home router but remain conceptually distinct.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module
Sending proceeds from application data to transport segment/datagram, network packet, link frame and physical bits/symbols; receiving reverses the order.
Each layer serves the layer above.
A router removes a received link frame, inspects IP, and creates a new link frame for the next hop.
MAC addresses usually change across routed hops; end-to-end IP addresses ordinarily remain until translation.
