notes.title: Link control, framing and error detection

blocks.text: Link-layer LLC identifies or multiplexes upper-layer protocols and may supply link control; MAC handles medium-dependent addressing/access and frame delivery.
Network addressing belongs to layer 3.
Ethernet, PPP and HDLC are link protocols.
Frame headers may carry addresses and control/type fields; synchronization and exact framing depend on the protocol.
Detection adds redundancy but does not guarantee correction.
Even parity adds a bit so the total number of ones is even: 1011 needs parity 1.
It detects every odd number of bit flips but misses even counts.
CRC treats bits as a polynomial and appends the XOR-division remainder; the receiver repeats the division.
Internet checksums add words with end-around carry and complement the sum.
A burst spans from the first corrupted bit through the last, including unchanged interior bits.
Retransmission or sufficient forward-error-correcting redundancy is needed for recovery.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module
Random access allows contention: ALOHA sends opportunistically; CSMA senses before sending.
In legacy half-duplex Ethernet, CSMA/CD detects collision, sends a jam indication, stops, and retries after random backoff.
The jam signals a collision, not its clearance.
Wi-Fi 802.11 uses CSMA/CA with waiting/backoff and acknowledgments; sensing does not eliminate hidden-terminal collisions.
Controlled access uses polling, reservations or a token to grant turns; correctly coordinated access avoids contention collisions.
Channelization divides frequency, time or code resources.
Stop-and-wait sends one frame and waits for ACK, retransmitting on timeout; sequence bits distinguish duplicates.
Sliding windows permit multiple unacknowledged frames.
Link reliability/flow control is hop-local; transport reliability/flow control is end-to-end.
Ethernet detects corruption but does not itself guarantee reliable delivery.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module
Line coding maps digital bits to digital signal patterns.
NRZ uses levels without a forced mid-bit return; Manchester supplies a mid-bit transition for clocking, with bit convention specified.
Differential Manchester encodes using transitions relative to previous state.
AMI alternates the polarity of successive ones; pseudoternary alternates zero pulses.
Block coding adds code redundancy; scrambling replaces problematic patterns without necessarily increasing bit count.
Multilevel schemes include 2B1Q and 8B6T; MLT-3 uses a sequence of voltage transitions.
ASK varies carrier amplitude, FSK frequency, PSK phase; QAM combines amplitude and phase.
AM/FM/PM can carry analog data.
PCM digitizes analog input by sampling, quantizing and encoding.

Sampling must exceed twice the highest retained baseband frequency in practical designs; b-bit samples have 2^b quantization levels and uncompressed rate fs×b. PAM/PWM are pulse modulation methods; pulse amplitude or width alone is not a binary PCM code.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module
IP supplies connectionless best-effort packet delivery, not end-to-end ordering or retransmission.
IPv4 addresses are 32 bits.
Its minimum header is 20 bytes and can grow to 60 bytes; it is not a 32-bit header.
IHL counts 32-bit words; total length includes header and payload.
TTL limits lifetime across routers; the protocol field identifies TCP, UDP or another upper-layer protocol.
The IPv4 checksum protects its header; IP does not lack error checking altogether.
Identification, flags and offset support fragmentation.
IPv4 sources and routers may fragment when allowed; reassembly occurs at the destination.
If DF is set and the next MTU is too small, forwarding fails and an ICMP diagnostic may be returned.
IETF RFC 791
TCP offers a reliable ordered byte stream using sequence numbers, acknowledgments, retransmission and windows.
Flow control protects the receiver; congestion control protects network capacity.
UDP sends independent datagrams with ports and a checksum but no built-in setup, delivery guarantee, retransmission or ordering.
Live interactive traffic may choose UDP when late data is less useful than lost data.
Application protocols can add reliability over UDP.
Ports identify transport endpoints; the application can choose a transport and request socket buffer sizes, subject to OS limits.
A TCP connection is identified by source/destination IP and source/destination port, with TCP understood.
IPv4 protocol numbers identify upper protocols; 80 is a usual HTTP port, not an IP protocol number.
Clients often use ephemeral ports.
SCTP is a reliable message-oriented transport with multiple streams.
IETF RFC 9293
TCP establishes state with SYN, SYN+ACK, then ACK.
SYN consumes one sequence position even with no application bytes.
An acknowledgment states the next expected sequence number.
For client ISN=395 and server ISN=260: client sends SYN seq395; server sends SYN+ACK seq260 ack396; client sends ACK seq396 ack261.
Later byte counts advance sequence numbers.
FIN also consumes one sequence position.
TCP setup creates a logical transport connection, not a reserved physical circuit.
Ports allow multiplexing separate applications over IP; they do not combine all applications into one TCP byte stream.
Do not assign TCP reliability to all layer-4 protocols merely because the reference layer lists reliability as a possible service.
IETF RFC 9293

notes.title: Upper layers and the TCP/IP correspondence

blocks.text: OSI session roles establish/manage dialogs and can coordinate checkpoints so transfer resumes after interruption.
Presentation roles translate encodings and handle compression/encryption.
Compression reduces representation size; encryption hides content and need not shrink it.
Application protocols provide services directly to applications.
Practical implementations distribute these functions differently; TLS is not proof of a separate physical presentation-layer device.
The four-layer TCP/IP model folds OSI layers 5–7 into application, retains transport, calls layer 3 Internet, and combines link/physical as network access.
A model is a guide to functions, not a guarantee that every application gets a reliable network.
Distinguish end-to-end application service from its underlying process-to-process transport.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module
DNS resolves names to records, including IPv4 A and IPv6 AAAA addresses; it can use UDP or TCP port 53.
DHCP dynamically leases IPv4 settings, commonly address, mask, gateway and DNS server.
Its basic exchange is discover, offer, request, acknowledge.
IP itself does not assign addresses.
ARP resolves an on-link IPv4 next hop to a link address, using a broadcast request and normally unicast reply.
For an off-subnet target, ARP resolves the gateway, not the remote target’s MAC.
It bridges the network/link addressing boundary and is often classified at the link layer; calling ARP simply a network protocol uses a loose textbook convention.
RARP reverses hardware-to-IP lookup; BOOTP/DHCP support boot configuration.
ICMP reports errors and diagnostics; IGMP manages IPv4 multicast membership.
These are separate companion protocols, not four pieces whose combination is IP.
IETF RFC 826

notes.title: Web, file, mail and remote-login protocols

blocks.text: HTTP defines web request/response semantics; it is stateless, and a message body may be absent.
HTTPS adds TLS protection.
FTP transfers files using control and separate data connections; it is not the same protocol as SFTP.
SMTP submits and relays mail; POP3 retrieves messages and IMAP accesses/synchronizes server mailboxes.
Saying SMTP handles both sending and end-user mailbox retrieval is inaccurate.
Usual service ports: FTP control 21, SSH 22, Telnet 23, SMTP relay 25, DNS 53, HTTP 80, POP3 110, IMAP 143, HTTPS 443.
Telnet provides unencrypted remote terminals; SSH protects remote access.
Servers can be configured on other ports.
A browser’s HTTP exchange does not determine the physical duplex mode of its network interface.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module
Write IPv4 as four decimal octets 0–255, or as 32 binary bits.
Use weights 128,64,32,16,8,4,2,1 within each octet.
A value such as 257 is impossible.
Syntactic validity differs from assignability: an address ending .0 or .255 can be a host under some prefixes.
Historical classes use leading patterns: A 0 with /8, B 10 with /16, C 110 with /24; D 1110 is multicast and E 1111 reserved.
Ordinary class-A first octets are 1–126 because 0 and 127 have special uses.
B spans 128–191 and C 192–223.
Default usable counts are 2^24-2, 2^16-2 and 254.
Modern CIDR requires the actual prefix and overrides class defaults.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module

notes.title: Special ranges, private addresses and IPv6

blocks.text: They can be reused internally but are not globally routed as public destinations.

A LAN may also use legitimately assigned public addresses; private is common, not mandatory. 127.0.0.0/8 is IPv4 loopback, commonly 127.0.0.1, for local protocol access without an external link. 255.255.255.255 is limited broadcast; 0.0.0.0 can identify an unconfigured source.
Link-local/APIPA uses 169.254.0.0/16, with edge /24 blocks excluded from normal automatic selection.
IPv6 has 128-bit hexadecimal addresses, flexible prefixes and no IPv4-style broadcast.
Sources, not routers, fragment IPv6 packets.
IPv6 does not automatically encrypt traffic or make authentication unnecessary.
Compare IPv6’s larger 128-bit address space and encryption support separately; specify the property being evaluated.
IETF RFC 1918
IETF RFC 8200
A /p IPv4 prefix has p leading one bits followed by 32-p zeros.
Compute network=address AND mask.
Host bits zero identify the block start; host bits one give broadcast.
With 172.16.28.252/20, the third octet is grouped in blocks of 16, so the network is 172.16.16.0 and broadcast 172.16.31.255.
A written host/prefix such as 172.105.180.0/21 need not be an aligned block label: masking yields 172.105.176.0/21.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module

notes.title: Find subnet bounds and usable hosts

blocks.text: For ordinary broadcast LANs let h=32-p. Total addresses=2^h; usable hosts=2^h-2, reserving network and directed broadcast.
Find the changing octet’s increment as 256-mask octet, round the address down to a multiple, and extend through the next boundary minus one.

192.168.2.64/26 spans .64–.127; usable .65–.126 gives 62 hosts. 192.168.10.25/28 spans .16–.31, so its network is .16. 172.17.128.0/21 spans 172.17.128.0–172.17.135.255; .128.255 and .135.0 are valid interior hosts, but .135.255 is broadcast. /27 gives 32 total and 30 usable, not 32 usable.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module

notes.title: Borrow bits and choose a mask

blocks.text: To split parent /a into equal /p blocks, borrow b=p-a bits and obtain 2^b subnets.
Do not subtract two subnets under modern practice.
For a Class B /16 parent split to /19, b=3 gives eight subnets, each with 8192 addresses and 8190 conventional hosts.
A /19 alone does not state its parent.
For H hosts, choose the smallest h satisfying 2^h-2≥H, then p=32-h. For 24 hosts use /27; 52 or 57 use /26; 100 use /25; 500 use /23.
For at least six equal subnets choose b=3.
A Class C /24 split to /27 yields eight subnets.
Always check both the number of subnets and the host capacity.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module

notes.title: Design and implement a VLSM address plan

blocks.text: VLSM assigns different masks to different LAN sizes.
Sort demands largest first, round each to a power-of-two address block including reservations, allocate aligned nonoverlapping blocks within the parent, and leave the remaining space explicit.
Two remote LANs of 100 each fit .0/25 and .128/25 within a separate /24.
Count router interfaces as hosts if not already included in the demand.

Implementation assigns unique usable IPs/masks, puts each default gateway in its local subnet, configures router interfaces/routes and DHCP exclusions, then tests local reachability, gateway reachability, remote routing and DNS separately.
Check duplicate addresses, overlap and return routes before blaming an application.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module
A conventional /30 has four addresses and two usable endpoints; check the link and addressing assumptions when selecting a WAN prefix.
RFC3021 permits /31 on supported point-to-point links: both addresses are endpoints, so the subtract-two rule does not apply. /32 identifies one address/host route.
Do not claim /30 is universally the smallest valid link prefix.
CIDR, Classless Inter-Domain Routing, replaces rigid class allocation and supports aggregation.
Combine contiguous aligned blocks sharing leading bits; unrelated adjacent-looking labels may not aggregate cleanly.
Four consecutive /26 blocks covering a /24 summarize to /24.
More-specific routes must remain available where the aggregate would otherwise send traffic to the wrong next hop.
IETF RFC 3021
IETF RFC 4632
Static NAT gives a fixed address mapping; dynamic NAT allocates mappings from a pool.
PAT/NAPT maps address-plus-port combinations so multiple private clients share a public address.
It is translation, not ARP resolution and not encryption.
Return traffic must match the translation state or a configured inbound mapping.
A private host such as 10.0.0.1 commonly reaches the public Internet through NAT at a gateway, together with valid routing and a public external address.
NAT alone does not supply a physical connection or DNS.
A public address does not automatically grant permission to use it; both public and private unicast addresses can be used on a LAN under the correct allocation and subnet.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module
Routing computes paths; forwarding chooses a next hop for an individual packet.
Select the matching route with the longest prefix, then apply the routing system’s tie-breaking criteria.
A default /0 matches when nothing more specific does.
Static routes are configured; dynamic protocols exchange reachability.
Distance vector uses neighbor estimates, while link state distributes link information and computes shortest paths.
Interior protocols operate within an autonomous system; BGP exchanges routes between systems.
Flooding sends copies on eligible outgoing links with duplicate/lifetime controls; random walk picks a neighbor probabilistically.
Unicast targets one destination, broadcast all in a scope, multicast a subscribed group and anycast one member sharing an address, normally nearest under routing metrics.
Multi-destination packets can list multiple targets; this is not necessarily identical to broadcast.
Group multicast trees use mechanisms such as reverse-path checks; Ethernet spanning tree is a different layer-2 mechanism.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module
Circuit switching sets up a path with reserved resources, transfers data, then releases it.
Predictable allocated bandwidth trades against setup/blocking and wasted reservation during silence.
A traditional telephone call is the standard example.
Packet switching divides data into packets that share links statistically; queueing can add variable delay and loss.
This does not make modern voice-over-packet impossible: buffering, scheduling and capacity planning manage it.
Datagram packets are forwarded independently.
Virtual circuits establish forwarding state, but resource reservation is optional, not a necessary property of every virtual circuit.
Message switching stores a complete message before forwarding, without a dedicated end-to-end path.
Packet store-and-forward waits for the full packet/frame; cut-through starts after enough header arrives; fragment-free historically waits through the initial collision-sensitive portion.
No routing algorithm guarantees that every packet always takes the geometrically shortest route.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module
Multiplexing combines multiple input streams onto a shared link; demultiplexing separates them at the receiver.
It differs from broadcasting one message to many destinations.
FDM assigns distinct frequency bands with suitable guard spacing; WDM assigns different optical wavelengths.
TDM allocates time slots: synchronous TDM reserves recurrent slots even if an input is idle, while statistical TDM allocates according to demand and needs identification.
FDMA and TDMA allocate frequencies or time among users; CDMA separates coded signals.
Physical multiplexing is different from transport port multiplexing.
Combining signals onto a shared link is multiplexing; distinguish it from point-to-point connectivity, broadcast, synchronization and multicast.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module

notes.title: Identify networking layers and addressing assumptions

blocks.text: First identify the exact layer, protocol and scope.
Flow/error control can exist at both link and transport layers; MAC addresses can be locally administered; bridges and switches both operate at layer 2.
A LAN can use public or private unicast space.
UDP and IP are both connectionless.
Session dialogs and TCP connections are distinct senses of connection.
Distinguish the protocol, layer and scope before treating these descriptions as exclusive.
A host address without a prefix does not determine capacity unless the question explicitly assumes historical classful addressing.
A subnet count needs a parent block.
Excluding subnet zero and the all-ones subnet is an obsolete convention; apply it only when explicitly stated.
Choose a networking concept by its definition rather than by repeated distractors.
Read complete, unambiguous option labels before matching them to networking concepts.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module

Adaptive or dynamic routing changes routes in response to updated network information; nonadaptive or static routing uses configured choices. Distributed routing means routers perform computations using exchanged information instead of requiring one central route computation. These properties do not imply random next-hop selection: the path-selection rule is a separate classification.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module · page 19
RFC 1058 — Distance-vector computation and topology changes

notes.title: Management, traffic service and application transport bindings

blocks.text: SNMP means Simple Network Management Protocol. Its management applications monitor and control managed devices, such as hosts and routers, by exchanging management information with their agents. This device-management role differs from transferring email, resolving names or mapping an IP address to a MAC address.

In the conventional service bindings, FTP control, SMTP mail transfer and Telnet remote terminals use TCP. DNS supports both UDP and TCP on port 53; it is not exclusively a UDP service. The application protocol’s service role is distinct from the transport carrying its messages.

Quality of service (QoS) controls traffic treatment to meet objectives such as throughput, delay, jitter or loss. Classification, queue scheduling and allocation of buffer or bandwidth resources implement such treatment. QoS concerns delivered service behavior; scalability concerns accommodating growth, and security concerns unauthorized actions.
RFC 3411 — SNMP architecture, section 1.2
Data Communication and Computer Networking module · page 28
RFC 2475 — Differentiated-services architecture

notes.title: Why IPv4 conservation and IPv6 matter

blocks.text: The finite IPv4 address space has faced allocation scarcity. Private addressing with NAT conserves public IPv4 addresses, while IPv6 provides a much larger address space.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module · page 19

A computer network connects computers or other devices so they can exchange information and share resources such as files, storage and printers. The interconnection uses both hardware and software; neither hardware alone nor software alone is the definition of the whole network.

NIC expands to Network Interface Card. It is the host’s network interface, providing the connection through which the host sends and receives network signals. A cable connector attaches the medium to that interface; it is distinct from an intermediary switch or router.
CRC expands to Cyclic Redundancy Check.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module · page 22
Data Communication and Computer Networking module · page 23
Data Communication and Computer Networking module · page 13

Ethernet and Token Ring are traditional LAN technologies. X.25 and Frame Relay are traditional WAN technologies. TCP/IP can run over different network-access technologies; its Internet-layer packet service does not require one particular link medium or frame format.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module · page 26

An IP address identifies a network interface rather than limiting a whole computer to one address. A computer or router can have several interfaces and addresses. Under a supplied IPv4 prefix, leading bits identify the network and the remaining bits identify an address within that network; a MAC address is a separate link-layer identifier.

TCP and UDP port fields are 16 bits, allowing numbers from 0 through 65535. Well-known ports are 0–1023, registered ports are 1024–49151, and dynamic/private ports are 49152–65535. Client endpoints can use dynamically selected ports instead of every application requiring a well-known assignment. These port numbers are distinct from the IP version and upper-protocol fields.

A bridge or switch’s MAC address table is its learned forwarding database: it associates MAC addresses with ports for frame forwarding. It differs from an ARP cache, which associates an IPv4 next hop with a link address, and from a routing table, which selects next hops for IP prefixes.

A common IPv6 unicast subnet uses a 64-bit subnet prefix and a 64-bit interface identifier. This split does not make the complete address 64 bits: it remains 128 bits. Special uses and explicitly different prefix lengths must be considered separately.
Data Communication and Computer Networking module · page 18
Data Communication and Computer Networking module · page 28
Cisco — Configure MAC address learning and forwarding tables
RFC 7421 — Analysis of the 64-bit boundary in IPv6 addressing

notes.title: Physical signaling and legacy Ethernet cable roles

blocks.text: Fiber-optic links can use near-infrared light. The selected optical wavelength is part of the link’s physical signaling specification, just as connectors and electrical signal levels are physical-interface specifications. This does not require every fiber link to use the same wavelength.

For legacy fixed Ethernet port roles, PCs and router Ethernet endpoints use the same endpoint role, while ordinary switch ports use the opposite role. Thus a direct router-to-PC link uses crossover wiring; PC-to-switch or router-to-switch uses straight-through wiring. Automatic MDI-X can remove the need to choose the crossover manually.

Ethernet switches can have fiber-optic interfaces with suitable optical transceivers. A forwarding role therefore does not impose a copper-only restriction: distinguish what the device does with frames from the physical medium used by its ports.

Intermodulation distortion occurs when multiple signals interact through a nonlinear component and generate unwanted combination-frequency products. Its mechanism differs from random thermal motion, adjacent-channel leakage and an isolated impulse disturbance.

note_intro.text: Learn how signals become frames, packets and application data, then practise address plans with explicit masks. This chapter develops all four blueprint outcomes through networking concepts and practical procedures.
Trace one message down and up the layers; distinguish MAC, IP and port addresses.
Calculate masks, network/broadcast bounds and capacity before looking at choices. Allocate largest LANs first and validate the full plan.
Use comparison tables and microexamples for retrieval practice, then explain why competing answers fail. Check the protocol, addressing and scope assumptions before selecting an answer.
